courses.title: Nuclear Medicine and Radiotherapy
courses.description: Radionuclides and radiopharmaceuticals, gamma camera and PET imaging procedures, radionuclide therapy, principles and practice of radiotherapy, and radiation safety in these departments.

topics.title: Radionuclides and Radiopharmaceuticals
topics.summary: Radioactive decay, half-life, generator systems, radiopharmaceutical properties and quality control.

material.heading: Decay and half-life
material.body: Radioactive decay modes: alpha (helium nuclei — high LET, short range; used in targeted therapy such as radium-223), beta-minus (electrons — therapy with iodine-131, lutetium-177, yttrium-90), beta-plus (positrons — PET imaging with fluorine-18, gallium-68), gamma emission (photons — imaging) and isomeric transition (technetium-99m). Activity is measured in becquerels (1 Bq = 1 disintegration per second; older unit curie, 1 mCi = 37 MBq). A = A0 e^(−λt); physical half-life (T½) — time for activity to halve; biological half-life — time for the body to eliminate half; effective half-life: 1/Teff = 1/Tphys + 1/Tbiol. The ideal diagnostic radionuclide has a short half-life (hours), emits gamma rays of 100–200 keV without particulate radiation, is cheap and readily available — technetium-99m (T½ 6 hours, 140 keV) meets these criteria and is used in about 80% of procedures.

material.heading: Generators and radiopharmaceuticals
material.body: The molybdenum-99/technetium-99m generator: Mo-99 (T½ 66 hours) adsorbed on an alumina column decays to Tc-99m, which is eluted ('milked') with saline as sodium pertechnetate; transient equilibrium allows daily elution for about a week. Radiopharmaceutical kits label Tc-99m to carriers: MDP (bone), MAG3 and DTPA (renal function), DMSA (renal cortex/scarring), MAA (lung perfusion), sestamibi/tetrofosmin (myocardial perfusion, parathyroid), HMPAO (brain perfusion, labelled leucocytes), sulfur colloid (liver/spleen, lymphoscintigraphy), and pertechnetate alone (thyroid, Meckel's diverticulum). Quality control: molybdenum breakthrough (limit about 0.15 µCi Mo-99 per mCi Tc-99m), aluminium breakthrough, radiochemical purity (chromatography — free pertechnetate and hydrolysed reduced technetium), sterility and apyrogenicity. Radiopharmacy must follow GMP and radiation protection (shielded hot lab, dose calibrator checks).
keyPoints: MDP bone; MAG3 renal; DMSA cortex

topics.title: Nuclear Medicine Imaging Procedures
topics.summary: Bone, renal, thyroid, cardiac, lung and PET studies: indications, preparation and interpretation.

material.heading: Common studies
material.body: Bone scan (Tc-99m MDP, images at 2–4 hours; hydration and voiding): detects metastases (breast, prostate — very common indication in Nigeria), osteomyelitis (three-phase scan), stress fractures and Paget's disease; a 'superscan' shows diffuse uptake with absent renal activity (widespread metastases). Renography: MAG3/DTPA with furosemide diuresis assesses obstruction (e.g. pelviureteric junction obstruction) and split renal function; DMSA for scarring. Thyroid scan (pertechnetate or I-123): hot (hyperfunctioning) versus cold nodules (cold nodules need FNAC), Graves' disease (diffuse increased uptake) versus thyroiditis (reduced uptake); patients stop thyroid medication and avoid iodine contrast beforehand. Myocardial perfusion imaging (sestamibi at stress and rest): reversible defects indicate ischaemia; fixed defects indicate infarction. Lung V/Q scanning for pulmonary embolism (mismatched perfusion defects), especially when CT contrast is contraindicated or in pregnancy. Gastrointestinal bleeding (labelled red cells) and Meckel's diverticulum (pertechnetate) studies.

material.heading: PET and patient care
material.body: PET/CT with F-18 FDG images glucose metabolism: staging and restaging of cancers (lymphoma, lung, colorectal, head and neck, melanoma), assessing treatment response, finding occult primaries and infection/inflammation. Patient preparation: fast 4–6 hours, blood glucose ideally < 11 mmol/L (hyperglycaemia reduces tumour uptake), avoid strenuous exercise for 24 hours, rest quietly after injection (uptake period about 60 minutes) to avoid muscle uptake, keep warm to reduce brown fat uptake. Physiological FDG uptake: brain, heart (variable), kidneys and bladder, bowel, and brown fat. Other PET tracers: Ga-68 PSMA (prostate cancer), Ga-68 DOTATATE (neuroendocrine tumours). Radiation protection for patients: pregnancy screening, breastfeeding advice (interrupt for some agents), minimise dose (justification, optimisation), and advice to minimise close contact with children after some procedures. Nigeria has a small number of nuclear medicine centres (e.g. UCH Ibadan, LUTH, NHA Abuja) and limited PET/CT capacity.

topics.title: Radionuclide Therapy
topics.summary: Radioiodine therapy, other therapeutic radionuclides, patient preparation and radiation protection.

material.heading: Radioiodine
material.body: Iodine-131 (T½ about 8 days; beta emitter for therapy with gamma emissions for imaging) is concentrated by the thyroid via the sodium–iodide symporter. Uses: hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease, toxic nodular goitre — about 200–600 MBq; may cause hypothyroidism requiring levothyroxine; may worsen Graves' ophthalmopathy — steroid cover) and differentiated thyroid cancer (ablation of thyroid remnant and treatment of metastases after total thyroidectomy — 1.1–5.5 GBq or more, with TSH stimulation by withdrawal of thyroxine or recombinant TSH, and a low-iodine diet). Contraindications: pregnancy and breastfeeding (must stop breastfeeding completely for the current child); women should avoid pregnancy for 6 months and men should avoid fathering children for about 4 months afterwards. Radiation protection after treatment: isolation in shielded rooms for high-dose therapy until activity falls below release limits, separate toilets, flushing twice, avoiding close contact with children and pregnant women for specified periods, and handling of contaminated waste and linen.
keyPoints: Thyroid cancer ablation with TSH stimulation

material.heading: Other therapies
material.body: Other radionuclide therapies (theranostics — using a diagnostic analogue to select patients for therapy): lutetium-177 PSMA (metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer), lutetium-177 DOTATATE (neuroendocrine tumours), radium-223 (alpha emitter for bone metastases from prostate cancer — improves survival), strontium-89 and samarium-153 (bone pain palliation), iodine-131 MIBG (neuroblastoma, phaeochromocytoma), yttrium-90 microspheres (selective internal radiation therapy for liver tumours), and radiosynovectomy for chronic synovitis. Side effects: myelosuppression, xerostomia (salivary uptake), nausea, and renal toxicity (with some agents). Staff protection: time, distance and shielding; personal dosimetry; handling in shielded syringes; spill procedures; and waste storage for decay. Therapies require licensing by the Nigerian Nuclear Regulatory Authority (NNRA).

topics.title: Principles of Radiotherapy
topics.summary: Radiobiology, fractionation, external beam equipment, brachytherapy and treatment planning.

material.heading: Radiobiology
material.body: Radiotherapy uses ionising radiation to kill cancer cells mainly by DNA damage (double-strand breaks) — directly or indirectly via free radicals from water (oxygen fixes the damage; hypoxic tumour cells are radioresistant — oxygen enhancement ratio). Dose is measured in gray (Gy = 1 J/kg). The 4 Rs of radiobiology explain fractionation (dividing the total dose into small daily fractions, e.g. 2 Gy per fraction, 5 days a week): Repair (normal tissues repair sublethal damage between fractions better than tumours), Repopulation (tumour regrowth during prolonged treatment — avoid unnecessary gaps), Redistribution (cells move into radiosensitive phases — G2/M), and Reoxygenation (hypoxic cells become oxygenated). A fifth R — radiosensitivity. The linear–quadratic model (α/β ratio: early-responding tissues and most tumours ~10 Gy; late-responding tissues ~3 Gy) guides fractionation; hypofractionation (fewer, larger fractions) is increasingly used (e.g. breast, prostate). Concurrent chemotherapy (cisplatin) sensitises tumours (e.g. cervical and head and neck cancers).

material.heading: Equipment and planning
material.body: External beam radiotherapy (teletherapy): cobalt-60 units (gamma rays 1.17 and 1.33 MeV; T½ 5.3 years — simpler, still used in some Nigerian centres) and linear accelerators (LINACs — megavoltage X-rays 6–18 MV and electrons; skin-sparing effect due to dose build-up below the surface). Advanced techniques: 3D conformal radiotherapy, intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT), volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT), image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) and stereotactic radiosurgery. Treatment planning: immobilisation (thermoplastic masks, vacuum bags), CT simulation, target volumes (GTV — gross tumour; CTV — clinical target including microscopic spread; PTV — planning margin for set-up uncertainty), organs at risk with dose constraints, dose calculation and plan verification. Brachytherapy places sealed sources inside or near the tumour (high dose-rate iridium-192 for cervical cancer — intracavitary; prostate seeds). Nigeria has very few radiotherapy centres relative to need, with frequent machine downtime.

topics.title: Radiotherapy Practice and Side Effects
topics.summary: Treatment delivery, verification, acute and late toxicities, patient care and safety.

material.heading: Delivery and verification
material.body: Therapy radiographers deliver radiotherapy accurately and safely: patient identification, consent and pregnancy checks, reproducible positioning using immobilisation devices, skin marks or tattoos and lasers, image guidance (portal imaging, cone-beam CT) to verify position before treatment, delivery of the prescribed fractions, and monitoring the patient's condition and side effects. Errors (wrong patient, wrong site, wrong dose — e.g. historical overdose incidents worldwide) are prevented through independent checks, record-and-verify systems, in vivo dosimetry, machine quality assurance (daily output checks, mechanical and safety interlocks) and incident reporting. The radiotherapy bunker has thick concrete walls (primary and secondary barriers), a maze, door interlocks and warning lights; no one other than the patient is in the room during treatment. Patient communication and psychological support are essential — radiotherapy is often misunderstood (fear of burns or becoming radioactive — external beam patients are not radioactive).

material.heading: Side effects
material.body: Side effects depend on site, dose and fractionation. Acute effects (during and a few weeks after treatment, rapidly dividing tissues): fatigue, skin reactions (erythema, dry and moist desquamation — keep the area clean and dry, gentle washing, avoid perfumed products, tight clothing, sun exposure and adhesive tapes; moisturisers as advised), mucositis (head and neck — oral care, analgesia, nutrition), diarrhoea (pelvic and abdominal RT), cystitis, nausea, and myelosuppression. Late effects (months to years, slowly dividing tissues; often irreversible): fibrosis, lymphoedema, xerostomia and dental caries (head and neck — dental assessment before RT; fluoride), osteoradionecrosis, radiation proctitis and cystitis, vaginal stenosis (dilators), infertility, cataract, pneumonitis/fibrosis, cardiac toxicity, hypothyroidism and second malignancies. Palliative radiotherapy (e.g. 8 Gy single fraction for painful bone metastases, whole-brain RT, haemostatic RT for bleeding tumours, spinal cord compression) relieves symptoms effectively. Nutrition and weight monitoring, smoking cessation and follow-up improve outcomes.
keyPoints: Skin care: gentle, dry, no perfumes
